summary: This unit teaches you to manage remuneration strategies and plans in a Jamaican public body or business. You will learn how pay supports the organisation's strategic plan, how jobs are evaluated and graded, how to compare pay with the market, how pay ranges and progression work, how to use performance pay, allowances and non-financial rewards, how to cost and introduce a pay plan fairly and legally, and how to evaluate whether it works.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification, with a public-sector code (PSA). It is for HR managers, supervisors and senior officers who design, cost, introduce or review pay arrangements in a ministry, agency, statutory body, municipal corporation or business. **Remuneration** means everything an employee is paid or given for doing the job: basic salary, allowances, benefits and other rewards. A **remuneration strategy** says how the organisation will use reward to help it achieve its plan. A **remuneration plan** puts that strategy into action: the grading structure, pay ranges, rules for progression, allowances, costs and timetable.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workplace
rows: State the aims, link them to the strategic plan, and set the principles and market position.
Use job descriptions and a job evaluation scheme to rank jobs fairly and place them in grades.
Use salary surveys and benchmark jobs to see how pay compares and decide the market position.
Set grades, ranges (minimum, midpoint, maximum), overlaps and rules for moving through the range.
Decide on performance pay, allowances, benefits and non-financial rewards that suit the organisation.
Observe minimum wage and equal pay law, statutory deductions, confidentiality and pay equity.
Calculate the cost, check affordability, consult, communicate, put people into the structure and run the payroll correctly.
Measure turnover, time to fill posts, equity and cost; review the strategy regularly.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with scenarios and calculations (compa-ratio, midpoints, spread, increases, costing, turnover).
A **written paper** with short answers and longer answers in full sentences.

**Group practical tasks**: evaluating and grading six jobs and proposing pay ranges from survey data; costing a pay review, working out compa-ratios and pay equity and presenting a recommendation to a role-played HR committee.

blocks.note: Remuneration questions are often sums plus judgement. Work out the figure, then say what it means for fairness, cost and the organisation's plan.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A remuneration strategy aims to **attract, keep and motivate** people with the skills the organisation needs, **fairly** and **within budget**. In a public agency it must also fit central government pay policy and approvals.

blocks.h: Linking the strategy to the strategic plan

blocks.p: If the strategic plan aims to build digital services, the remuneration strategy should help the body attract and keep scarce digital skills. If the plan aims to improve service to the public, reward should support the behaviour and skills that deliver it. Ask for each goal: what people and skills are needed, and what reward arrangements will bring and keep them?

blocks.h: Principles of a good pay system

head: Principle
Meaning
Example
rows: Jobs of equal value are paid equally, and more demanding jobs are paid more
Two officers doing jobs of the same size are in the same grade, whatever each negotiated at hiring
Pay is in line with what other employers pay for similar jobs
Using survey data to set the market position
Total cost stays within the approved budget
A phased pay plan that fits the salary budget
Follows the minimum wage, equal pay, tax and employment law
Equal pay for women and men doing equal work
Staff understand how pay is set and how to ask for a review
Clear rules applied the same way to everyone
Rules for starting pay and increments

blocks.p: **Total rewards** means everything the employer offers: pay, benefits, development, recognition and working conditions.

head: Component
Examples
rows: Salary or wage for the grade
Travel allowance, acting allowance, market (scarce-skills) allowance
Flexible hours, equipment, safe workplace, wellbeing support

blocks.p: **Worked example.** An officer has a basic salary of J$3,200,000, allowances of J$420,000 and employer-paid health insurance of J$180,000 a year. The value of her package is J$3,200,000 + J$420,000 + J$180,000 = **J$3,800,000** a year.

A public agency usually cannot set its own pay scales freely. Pay is set within central government policy, the approved budget and approvals from the parent ministry or the central body for public service compensation. The agency's job is to apply these rules fairly, add local detail where it is allowed (such as allowances for specific roles) and explain the rules to staff. Always check the current rules and approvals before making a pay proposal.

blocks.note: Where the agency cannot raise basic pay, it has other levers: allowances approved under the rules, development, flexible working and recognition. Non-financial rewards matter: exit interviews often show that people leave because of poor management, no development or inflexible hours, not only pay.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: Job evaluation: pay for the job, not the person

blocks.p: **Job evaluation** is a systematic process for judging the **relative size or value of jobs** in an organisation so that a fair grading structure can be built. It rates the **job**, not the person who holds it, and not how well that person performs. Performance is dealt with through appraisal.

Every job to be evaluated needs an **accurate, current job description**, agreed with the jobholder and the manager. Out-of-date descriptions lead to wrong grades. If a description still shows duties from five years ago, update it with the jobholder and manager before scoring.

head: Method
How it works
Points
rows: Jobs are put in order of importance
Simple but hard to explain or defend; not analytical
Jobs are matched to ready-made grade descriptions
Each job is scored on factors (knowledge, problem-solving, responsibility, contacts, working conditions); points are added
Analytical, consistent and explainable; most widely used
Jobs are valued by what the market pays
Reflects competitiveness; can reproduce existing unfairness

flow: Agree the purpose and scheme with senior management and the union or staff association
Set up a **trained panel** with members from different departments, women and men, and a union observer
Collect or update accurate job descriptions, checked by jobholders and managers
Evaluate a set of **benchmark jobs** first, to test the scheme
Score every job on each factor by panel consensus, and **record the reasons**
Add the points and rank the jobs
Draw **grade boundaries** at natural gaps in the points
Check the results for oddities and for any pattern that disadvantages women or one group
Tell staff the outcome, and provide an appeal process

blocks.p: **Worked example.** A job scores: knowledge 160, problem-solving 120, accountability 150, working conditions 30. Total = 160 + 120 + 150 + 30 = **460 points**. If Grade 5 covers 400 to 499 points and Grade 6 covers 500 to 599, the job is in **Grade 5**. A job with 499 points and one with 500 points are almost identical in size, yet are in different grades: that is why boundaries should be drawn at natural gaps and checked.

ul: Use the same factors for every job.
Train the evaluators; record reasons for every score.
Include women and men and different departments on the panel; check for gender bias.
Evaluate the job as it is, not the person: an officer who works very hard does not make her job larger. Hard work is rewarded through appraisal and progression.

Never grade a post higher to suit a person. If a senior officer asks for a relative's or friend's post to be graded higher than the evaluation shows, **refuse, keep to the evaluation and report the request** under the code of conduct.
Tell staff how the scheme works and give them an appeal route.

blocks.note: Equal pay law requires equal pay for women and men doing the same work or work of equal value. A sound, analytical job evaluation is the main way to show that jobs of equal value are paid equally.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: External competitiveness: salary surveys and market position

blocks.p: If an agency keeps losing officers to private firms, first compare its pay with reliable survey data for similar jobs. This shows whether pay is a cause, and by how much.

ul: A **salary survey** collects what other employers pay for similar jobs.
Surveys use **benchmark jobs**: common, clearly defined jobs that can be matched across employers. Match on **job content**, not on job title: the same title can describe quite different jobs.
A reliable survey has enough employers (a survey of only two employers is a weak basis), is recent, and covers similar organisations (size, sector, location).
Public bodies may also use official comparator data and central guidance.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: The middle value: half the rates are higher and half lower
Three-quarters of rates are below this value
A quarter of rates are below this value
Total ÷ number; can be pulled up by a few very high rates

blocks.p: The **market position** (pay policy line) is where the organisation chooses to pay relative to the market. An organisation may pay at the median for most jobs and at the 75th percentile for scarce skills such as IT. This is setting different market positions for different job groups.

head: Policy
Meaning
Effect
rows: Attracts and keeps staff; costs more
Cheaper; risk of losing staff; may need other rewards

blocks.p: **Worked example.** The median pay in the survey for a job is J$3,000,000 and the agency pays J$2,850,000. The gap is J$150,000. J$150,000 ÷ J$3,000,000 × 100 = **5% below** the market median.

blocks.h: Responding to market pressure within public rules

head: Option
Advantage
Risk
rows: Raise salaries for the job group
May damage internal equity; needs approval; costs every year
Easier to approve and to remove; reviewed each year
Needs clear rules so other groups see it as fair
Non-pay rewards (training, flexible work, career path)
Matters to many staff; costs less
Does not close a large pay gap alone
Retention payment for staying a set time
Keeps people through a key period

blocks.p: A sensible recommendation is often a mix: a reviewed scarce-skills allowance approved under the rules, with development and flexible working, and turnover measured over the next year.

After job evaluation, jobs of similar size are placed in **grades**. Each grade has a **pay range**: a **minimum**, a **midpoint** and a **maximum**. The midpoint is usually set at or near the market rate for a fully competent officer.

ul: 100% means pay is at the midpoint.
Below 100%: pay is below the midpoint. A new officer is naturally here; an experienced, well-performing officer here may be underpaid and likely to leave.
Above 100%: pay is above the midpoint; near the maximum, there is little room for future increases.
If most officers in one grade have compa-ratios of about 85% while the market has moved up, they are paid well below the midpoint and retention may suffer.
If most officers are about 110%, the organisation may have over-progressed staff, which limits its budget for future increases.
Look at compa-ratios by gender and group as well as overall.

blocks.p: Ranges for neighbouring grades often **overlap**, so an experienced officer at the top of one grade can earn more than a newcomer at the bottom of the next. For example, Grade 5 is J$2,400,000 to J$3,300,000 and Grade 6 is J$2,900,000 to J$3,900,000. The overlap is J$2,900,000 to J$3,300,000. Overlap rewards experience, but too much overlap blurs the difference between grades.

**Broadbanding** replaces many narrow grades with a few wide pay bands (for example 14 grades replaced by 5 bands). It gives managers more flexibility, but it needs clear rules and good management, or pay can drift and become unequal.

head: System
How it works
Strengths and weaknesses
rows: Officers move up by set steps, usually each year, if work is satisfactory
Simple, predictable, seen as fair; rewards time served, not results
Rewards results; needs a trusted appraisal system
Pay rises as skills are gained

blocks.p: **Worked example.** An officer earning J$2,400,000 gets a merit increase of 6%. Increase = J$2,400,000 × 6% = J$144,000. New salary = **J$2,544,000**.

head: Term
Situation
Usual approach
rows: Present salary is **above the maximum** of the new grade
Protect pay for a set period; no increase until the range catches up; may be reviewed with the officer
Present salary is **below the minimum** of the grade the job has been evaluated into
Raise to the minimum, often in steps if cost is high

blocks.p: Both are common when a new structure is introduced. Handle them by clear rules, approved in advance, applied the same way to everyone.

sections.title: Performance pay, allowances, benefits and non-financial rewards

blocks.p: Linking part of pay to performance can motivate staff and signal what the organisation values. But it works only with the right foundations.

head: Needs
Risks if missing
rows: A sound, trusted **appraisal system** with clear targets and trained managers
Seen as biased; disputes and grievances
Awards cannot be paid; staff lose trust
Staff are rewarded for what is easy to measure, not what matters
Team-based elements where teams depend on each other
Individual awards can weaken teamwork and encourage competition

blocks.p: In public bodies, where results are often shared and hard to measure for one person, these risks are real. A sensible recommendation is to keep service-based increments linked to a satisfactory appraisal, and add a modest team-based or individual award for outstanding performance once the appraisal system is shown to be sound.

An **allowance** is extra pay for a particular circumstance. Examples: travel allowance for use of own vehicle on field visits; acting allowance; market (scarce-skills) allowance; responsibility allowance; shift allowance.

The plan should make clear for each allowance: **who qualifies, the rate, how it is reviewed and what records are needed**, so that it is applied fairly and can be audited. Value is added to the total package: for example, a travel allowance of J$30,000 a month is worth 12 × J$30,000 = **J$360,000** a year.

ul: Health insurance, pension, paid leave, uniforms, training support.
Count the cost (employer-paid) when working out total rewards and total cost.
Some benefits are set by law or central policy; others are chosen by the organisation.

blocks.p: When a parish council or agency cannot raise pay this year, it can still help keep good staff:

ul: training and study support that lead to qualifications and promotion;
clear career paths and acting opportunities;
flexible start times or compressed hours where the service allows;
regular recognition: thanks, awards, public acknowledgement;
better equipment and working conditions;
wellbeing support.

blocks.p: Ask staff what they value through a short survey. Apply non-financial rewards fairly with clear rules, and check their effect through turnover and staff surveys.

sections.title: Legal requirements, pay equity and ethics

ul: **Minimum wage law:** wages must be at or above the national minimum wage at the current rate. Check it when costing the lowest grades and any part-time or contract work.
**Equal pay law:** women and men must be paid equally for the same work or work of equal value.

**Statutory deductions and employer contributions** (income tax, national insurance and other statutory payments, at the current rates). Deductions come out of the employee's pay; **employer contributions are added to the cost** of the pay plan.
**Employment law and contracts:** changes to pay or conditions must follow the law and any collective agreement.
**Data protection law:** pay and personal details are personal data and must be kept secure and shared only with those who need them for their role.
**Public finance rules:** public bodies must work within the approved budget and the central pay policy.

flow: Gather pay data for every officer: grade, salary, allowances, start date, performance rating, gender. Keep it secure; give access to a small authorised team
Compare the average and median pay of women and men in each grade and in jobs of equal value
Where gaps appear, **find the reasons**: starting salaries, faster progression for some groups, uneven allowances, jobs mainly done by women graded too low
Judge whether each reason is fair (for example length of service)
Correct unjustified gaps with a costed plan: raising pay in steps, regrading after evaluation, clear rules for starting pay and allowances
Report to senior management, inform staff in general terms without naming anyone, and repeat each year

blocks.p: **Worked example.** Men in a grade average J$2,600,000 and women average J$2,340,000. Gap = J$260,000. As a percentage of men's pay: 260,000 ÷ 2,600,000 × 100 = **10%**. The first step is to find the reasons, and check them for fairness.

A manager who asks HR for a spreadsheet of all salaries 'to get a feel for the numbers' should receive only what his role needs. Share the **structure** (grades, ranges, rules) widely; keep **individual** pay confidential.

ul: Grade and pay posts by the evaluation and the rules, not by who holds them.
Refuse requests to favour relatives or friends, and report them under the code of conduct.
Keep to the rules on starting pay and allowances, so that decisions can be explained and defended.
**Pay bill** = number of staff × average pay. A 5% increase = pay bill × 5%.
Add **employer contributions** and other costs that rise with pay (pension, overtime, pay-linked allowances), at the current rates.
Work out the **full-year** cost and the **part-year** cost if it starts mid-year.
Count the cost in **future years**: an increase to basic pay carries forward and raises the base for later increases.
Compare with the approved salary budget and central pay policy; find out which approvals are needed.

blocks.p: **Worked example.** An agency has 80 staff with an average salary of J$2,750,000. Pay bill = 80 × J$2,750,000 = J$220,000,000. A 5% increase costs J$220,000,000 × 5% = **J$11,000,000** a year in basic pay. If it starts on 1 October and the budget year runs from April to March, the first-year cost is for 6 of 12 months: J$11,000,000 ÷ 2 = **J$5,500,000**; from the next year, the full J$11,000,000. Employer contributions are then added at the current rates.
Another example: a pay bill of J$150,000,000 rising by 4% costs J$150,000,000 × 4% = J$6,000,000.

If a proposed structure costs more than the approved budget, do not simply go ahead. **Phase it in** (for example half the increase now, half next year), target the money (for example scarce skills and officers low in their ranges), or adjust the design, and obtain the approvals needed. A flat percentage for everyone is not always the fairest choice.

Where staff are represented by a union or staff association, **consult and negotiate** as the agreements and law require. Brief managers, listen to concerns, and explain the reasons. Good consultation improves the plan and reduces resistance.

blocks.h: Putting people into the new structure

flow: Confirm the budget and approvals in writing, and set a start date that gives payroll time to prepare
Place each officer in a grade from the job evaluation, and decide where they sit in the range under agreed rules
Raise officers below their new minimum (possibly in steps); protect those above their new maximum for a set period
Write to each officer: their grade, pay, how they will progress and how to appeal
Brief managers first, then hold staff sessions
Payroll checks **every new rate** before the first run; a second person checks a sample
Open an appeals process with time limits
Review at three and twelve months: appeals, cost, turnover and staff views

ul: Tell each officer how the structure works, their own grade and pay, and how to appeal.

An officer who thinks the job is in the wrong grade should have a **clear review process with set time limits**. Re-evaluate the job on the same factors using fresh evidence, with an independent panel, and give reasons for the outcome.
Staff often ask to see everyone's pay. Share the structure and rules; keep individual salaries confidential.

blocks.p: A strategy is judged by whether it achieves its aims. Set measures when you write it, and review regularly.

head: Aim
Measures
Source
rows: Time to fill posts; number and quality of applicants; offers refused because of pay
Turnover (overall and in scarce skills); reasons in exit interviews
Staff survey results on pay and recognition; grading appeals and grievances; pay equity review
Pay compared with up-to-date survey data; compa-ratios
Actual pay bill compared with budget and plan

blocks.p: **Turnover rate = leavers ÷ average number employed × 100.** An agency employs an average of 150 officers and 21 leave: 21 ÷ 150 × 100 = **14%**. Look at turnover for **high performers** and **scarce skills**, not only overall.

ul: Report findings to senior management with clear conclusions.
Review the strategy **regularly** (for example every year) and **when markets, budgets or the strategic plan change**.

Aim the next pay review at the problems found: more for scarce skills if those officers are leaving; correct unfair gaps; adjust ranges if many staff are low in them; improve non-pay rewards staff value, all within the budget.

blocks.note: Do not judge the strategy by one number. A low turnover may hide unhappy staff who cannot find other jobs; a high turnover in one group may be a pay problem or a management problem. Use several measures, and exit interviews.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: state the purpose of a remuneration strategy and link it to the strategic plan;
name the principles of a good pay system and explain internal equity and external competitiveness;
list the components of total rewards and value a package;
explain job evaluation, the point-factor method and how to keep evaluation fair;
use salary surveys, benchmark jobs, the median and market position, and compare pay with the market;
work out the midpoint, range spread and compa-ratio, and explain what they show;
explain overlap, broadbanding, increments, merit and red and green circles;
describe the conditions and risks of performance-related pay;
describe allowances, benefits and non-financial rewards, and say what a plan must state about an allowance;
explain the legal requirements (minimum wage, equal pay, statutory deductions and contributions, data protection) by their purpose;
carry out a pay equity review and calculate a gap;
cost a pay increase for a full and a part year and say what else must be added;
plan consultation, implementation, communication and appeals;
evaluate the strategy with turnover, time to fill, equity and cost, and decide what the next review should target;
refuse to grade or pay by favour.

terms: Everything paid or given to an employee for doing the job: pay, allowances and benefits
Pay, benefits, development, recognition and working conditions together
Fairness in pay between jobs of similar value inside the organisation
A systematic process of judging the relative size of jobs to build a fair grading structure
A job evaluation method that scores jobs on factors and adds the points
A common, clearly defined job that can be matched across employers in a salary survey
A study of what other employers pay for similar jobs
The middle value: half the rates above, half below
Where the organisation chooses to pay relative to the market
The minimum, midpoint and maximum for a grade
(Minimum + maximum) ÷ 2; usually the market rate for a fully competent officer
Replacing many narrow grades with a few wide pay bands
A fixed step by which pay rises within a scale, usually yearly
Pay above the maximum of the new grade; protected for a set period
Pay below the minimum of the grade; raised to the minimum, often in steps
Negotiation of pay and conditions between an employer and a union on behalf of staff
A check on whether pay differs unfairly between groups, such as women and men
Statutory payments the employer makes on top of an employee's pay, which add to the cost

c1.title: IT officers leaving a regional authority in Montego Bay
c1.text: A regional authority in Montego Bay has lost four IT officers in a year to private firms. The HR manager obtains a salary survey, but it covers only two employers. For the benchmark job of systems officer, the survey median is J$3,000,000 and the authority pays J$2,850,000. Central policy does not allow the authority to raise basic pay scales on its own, but it can propose allowances for named scarce-skill jobs. Exit interviews mention pay, but also a lack of training and no flexible working.

c2.title: A job evaluation panel in Mandeville
c2.text: An agency in Mandeville is evaluating 150 jobs with a point-factor scheme. The panel has members from several departments, both women and men, and a union observer. One job scores knowledge 160, problem-solving 120, accountability 150 and working conditions 30. Grade 5 covers 400 to 499 points and Grade 6 covers 500 to 599. The job description for one post still lists duties from five years ago. An officer, Tamara, says her job should be graded higher because she works longer hours than anyone else.

c3.title: Pay ranges in a ministry in Kingston
c3.text: In a Kingston ministry, Grade 5 has a range of J$2,400,000 to J$3,300,000 and Grade 6 has a range of J$2,900,000 to J$3,900,000. An officer in Grade 5 earns J$2,565,000. A Grade 6 officer, Janelle, earns J$3,740,000. After the new structure, one long-serving officer's present salary of J$3,500,000 is above the maximum of the grade in which her job now falls.

c4.title: Costing a pay review at a statutory body in Spanish Town
c4.text: A statutory body in Spanish Town has 80 staff with an average salary of J$2,750,000. Management proposes a 5% increase from 1 October; the budget year runs from April to March. A pay equity check shows that men in the grade average J$2,600,000 and women average J$2,340,000, a gap of 10% of men's pay. The union is represented by a local branch.

c5.title: Introducing a new structure at a municipal corporation in Trelawny
c5.text: A municipal corporation in Trelawny has approved a new pay structure. An average of 150 officers were employed last year and 21 left. After the structure is introduced, an officer, Marlon, believes his post has been placed in the wrong grade. Staff are also asking to see a list of everyone's salaries.

questions.q: What is the authority's pay position against the survey median for the systems officer job?
o: 5% above the market median
15% below the market median
5% below the market median
0.5% below the market median
questions.why: Gap = J$3,000,000 - J$2,850,000 = J$150,000. Percentage = 150,000 / 3,000,000 x 100 = 5% below the median. The calculation uses the market figure as the base.

questions.q: Why should the HR manager match survey jobs on content rather than on job title?
o: The same title can describe jobs of different size, so match on duties
Titles are always kept secret by employers who take part in surveys
Job titles in surveys are decided by the union and cannot be changed
Titles are shorter than job descriptions, so they save time in matching
questions.why: Employers use the same titles for different jobs. A benchmark job is matched by its duties, responsibility and skills. Matching by title can make pay look higher or lower than it really is.

questions.q: The survey covers only two employers. What is the main risk?
o: Two employers always give a median that is much too high
The union will refuse to accept any figure that comes from a survey
The survey cannot be used because surveys must cover all employers
It may not show the true market, so more sources are needed
questions.why: A reliable survey draws on enough similar employers and is recent. Two employers may be unusual. Use further surveys or official comparator data before basing a pay decision on the result.

questions.q: Which response best fits the authority's limits and the exit-interview findings?
o: Raise every IT salary above the market median without asking for any approval
A reviewed scarce-skills allowance, plus training and flexible working
Do nothing, since pay is the only reason people leave for private firms
Give a one-off cash gift to every employee in the authority this year
questions.why: A targeted allowance for scarce skills works within central rules and can be reviewed, while development and flexible working answer reasons given in exit interviews. Raising pay without approval breaks the rules, and a gift to everyone is not targeted.

questions.q: Into which grade does the job with 160, 120, 150 and 30 points fall?
o: Grade 6, with a total of 460 points
Grade 5, with a total of 460 points
Grade 5, with a total of 440 points
Grade 6, with a total of 520 points
questions.why: Total = 160 + 120 + 150 + 30 = 460 points. Grade 5 covers 400 to 499, so the job is in Grade 5. Always add the factor scores before placing the job in a grade.

questions.q: Why does the panel include women and men, several departments and a union observer?
o: It lets the panel score jobs faster than a smaller group could
It means that the panel does not need to record reasons for scores
It allows each panel member to score only his or her own department
It helps make the evaluation fair, balanced and trusted by staff
questions.why: A mixed, trained panel reduces bias, brings different views of the jobs and gives staff confidence in the result. Reasons for each score must still be recorded, and every job is scored on the same factors.

questions.q: How should the panel reply to Tamara's claim that her job deserves a higher grade because she works longer hours?
o: Explain that the job is rated, not the person; effort is dealt with in appraisal
Raise the grade, since hard work is the most important factor in any job scoring
Raise the grade by one step for each hour a week that she works above the norm
Refuse to discuss it with her until the whole evaluation exercise is finished
questions.why: Job evaluation measures the size of the job against the scheme's factors. A person's effort or hours do not change the job's size; they are recognised through appraisal and progression. She should be told how to appeal if she disagrees with the result.

questions.q: What should be done about the job description that still lists duties from five years ago?
o: Score the job from the old description and correct it later if needed
Score it from the panel's own idea of what the job should be
Update it with the jobholder and the manager before the job is scored
Leave the job out of the exercise and give it the lowest grade
questions.why: Evaluation depends on an accurate, current job description agreed with the jobholder and manager. An out-of-date description would give a wrong score and an unfair grade.

questions.q: What is the midpoint of the Grade 5 range?
questions.why: Midpoint = (minimum + maximum) / 2 = (2,400,000 + 3,300,000) / 2 = J$2,850,000. J$900,000 is the width of the range.

questions.q: What is the compa-ratio of the Grade 5 officer earning J$2,565,000?
questions.why: Compa-ratio = salary / midpoint x 100 = 2,565,000 / 2,850,000 x 100 = 90%. She is paid 10% below the midpoint. She may be new in the grade, or may be underpaid if experienced.

questions.q: A Grade 6 officer, Janelle, earns J$3,740,000. What is her compa-ratio and what does it suggest?
o: 110%; she is below the midpoint, so she is likely to leave for another employer
90%; she is above the midpoint, so there is less room for future increases
90%; she is below the midpoint, so the budget has plenty of room for increases
110%; she is above the midpoint, so there is less room for future increases
questions.why: Midpoint of Grade 6 = (2,900,000 + 3,900,000) / 2 = J$3,400,000. Compa-ratio = 3,740,000 / 3,400,000 x 100 = 110%. Pay above the midpoint leaves less room before the maximum, so future increases must be planned with care.

questions.q: What is the range spread of the Grade 5 range?
questions.why: Range spread = (maximum - minimum) / minimum x 100 = (3,300,000 - 2,400,000) / 2,400,000 x 100 = 37.5%. Dividing by the maximum gives 27.3%, which is a different measure.

questions.q: What is the yearly cost of the 5% increase in basic pay?
questions.why: Pay bill = 80 x J$2,750,000 = J$220,000,000. A 5% increase = J$220,000,000 x 5% = J$11,000,000 a year. J$220,000,000 is the whole pay bill, not the cost of the increase.

questions.q: What is the cost of the increase in the first budget year if it starts on 1 October?
o: J$11,000,000, because pay is always counted for twelve months
J$2,750,000, because only one quarter of the year is affected
J$5,500,000, because only half the staff are paid the increase
J$5,500,000, because only six months of the year fall after the start date
questions.why: From 1 October to 31 March is six months. First-year cost = J$11,000,000 x 6/12 = J$5,500,000. From the next year the full J$11,000,000 applies.

questions.q: Which reason for the pay gap could HR justify on fair grounds after checking the evidence?
o: Longer service among the men, with increments earned under the published scale
Higher starting pay agreed case by case with male recruits who asked for more
Jobs mainly done by women having been graded lower without any evaluation
Allowances paid to men in the grade but not offered to women doing the same work
questions.why: Length of service under a published scale is a fair, explainable cause, provided the records show it. Case-by-case starting pay, unevaluated grading of women's jobs and unequal allowances are the usual unjustified causes and should be corrected.

questions.q: What must be added to the J$11,000,000 to find the true yearly cost of the increase?
o: The cost of the deductions taken from employees' pay
Nothing, because basic pay is the only cost of an increase
Employer contributions and other pay-linked costs, at the current rates
The profit that the body makes in the year of the increase
questions.why: Employer contributions, pension and pay-linked allowances rise with basic pay and add to the cost. Deductions come out of the employee's pay and are not a cost on top. A public body does not make profit for this purpose.

questions.q: What was the turnover rate for last year?
questions.why: Turnover = leavers / average number employed x 100 = 21 / 150 x 100 = 14%. Using 100 instead of the average number gives an incorrect answer.

questions.q: How should Marlon's appeal about his grade be handled?
o: Through the appeal process, with a fresh evaluation by an independent panel
The HR manager decides alone, on the day that Marlon makes his appeal to her
The union decides the grade on the basis of how long he has served
His grade is changed at once, since appeals are always upheld in the first month
questions.why: A fair appeal process has set time limits, uses the same scheme and factors with fresh evidence, and is decided by evaluators who were not on the first panel. Reasons are given for the outcome.

questions.q: How should HR reply to the request to publish everyone's salary?
o: Publish the full list of names and salaries on the staff notice board
Refuse to share anything, including the grade structure and the ranges
Give the list to one trusted officer from each department only
Share the structure and rules widely; keep individual salaries confidential
questions.why: Staff are entitled to understand how pay is set, so the structure, ranges and rules are shared. Individual pay is personal data and is shown only to those whose role requires it, in line with the data protection law.

questions.q: An officer's pay is J$2,300,000 and the minimum of her grade is J$2,400,000. Her employer raises her to the minimum in two equal yearly steps. How large is the first step?
questions.why: The shortfall is J$2,400,000 - J$2,300,000 = J$100,000. In two equal steps, each is J$50,000. Officers whose pay is below the minimum of their grade are sometimes called green circles; raising them in steps eases the cost.
